processing: Leaves and young shoots of a small evergreen mountain rhododendron are dried without further processing.
harvest_season: The shrub flowers in June and July; little is recorded on an agreed picking time for the tea.
appearance_dry: Small, narrow, leathery leaves, matte green above and rusty beneath, with bits of twig.
appearance_liquor: Little is recorded on the cup; as with other dried leaf herbs, expect a clear golden-yellow.
appearance_wet: Small, firm green-brown leaves that keep their shape.
taste_profile: Known mainly as a fragrant, invigorating herb, with one Russian name meaning fragrant wild rosemary; a resinous herbal cup is what the plant suggests, but detailed tasting notes are scarce.

brewing.notes: A cautious starting point, not an established recipe. Use a small pinch, and treat it as a potent herb rather than a daily tea; ask a doctor first if pregnant or on medication.

vintage_note: Sold without vintage, in small packs by weight, mostly by Siberian and Buryat herb sellers. The species is listed in several regional Red Books in Russia, so wild-gathered supply deserves a question about where it came from.
description:
Sagan-dailya is a herbal tea from Rhododendron adamsii, a low mountain shrub of Eastern Siberia, Yakutia, Transbaikalia and Mongolia, growing on stony slopes at the upper forest line. In Buryat it is sagaan dali, and the spelling sagan-dailya, though common outside Buryatia, is a garbling of that name.

The tea is simply the dried leaf and shoot. The leaves are tiny, about 1 to 2 cm long, leathery and rust-scaled underneath, which is an easy way to recognise the genuine plant.

It is known above all as a tonic, and drinkers treat it as a strong herb. Start with a pinch and a short steep. Detailed tasting notes are scarce, though one of its folk names, fragrant wild rosemary, points to a scented cup.

This plant has real chemistry: it contains compounds related to cannabigerol and cannabichromene. That is a reason for moderation, not a selling point, and marketing built on it deserves suspicion.
history:
The plant appears in Tibetan medical writing under the names ba-lu and da-li. The 17th-century treatise by the Mongolian physician Zhambaldorzhi names its flower da-li and its leaves ba-lu, advises gathering white-flowered plants, and includes a stylised drawing.

The Buryat name likely descends from this: sagaan means white, so sagaan dali is white da-li, later reinterpreted as white wing. Russian settlers around Lake Baikal and in the Sayan had their own names, including Belogorsky tea. It has grown in the Moscow Botanical Garden of the Academy of Sciences since 1964.
